segments.english: There are four types in giving charity. One who wants to give but wants others not to give has an evil eye toward what belongs to others. One who wants others to give but himself not to give has an evil eye toward his own. One who wants to give and wants others to give is pious. One who wants neither himself nor others to give is wicked.

grammar: מִדּוֹת here means 'types, patterns'; the series 'four types' recurs in 5:14-15 (and 5:10-12).
The participle הָרוֹצֶה with the relative שֶׁ is a headless relative: 'the one who wants that ...'.
The imperfects יִתֵּן / יִתְּנוּ after שֶׁ express what is wanted; after the first clause the verb 'wants' is understood.
עֵינוֹ רָעָה, 'his eye is evil', is the idiom for grudgingness; בְּשֶׁל is the Mishnaic genitive 'in that which is of'.
The four types are given as bare predicates (חָסִיד, רָשָׁע): the first two have an evil eye, the third is pious, the fourth wicked.
segments.note: The mishnah gives the first two types no label beyond 'evil eye'; the English keeps this. In the second, third and fourth types the Hebrew has bare imperfects, and הָרוֹצֶה is understood from the first clause. The English supplies 'wants' in all three, as Rambam reads the third (the pious man is not content that he alone shows mercy but wants others to show it too). The pack's BDB entries for אַרְבַּע (Arba, a name), מִדָּה (tribute), עַיִן (Ain, a place) and אַחַר (the adverb 'after') are the wrong words. The tokens are pointed to the Jastrow entries the pack lists, or carry no sense.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: 'four types in the giving of charity', not literally 'in givers of charity', since one type does not give; likewise the next mishnah means 'in the going to the house of study'.

Bartenura: the first has an evil eye because he knows that charity enriches and does not want others enriched. Another explanation: he spares his relatives' money more than his own and does not want them to lose it, like the evil eye 'in his own' below.
Rambam: see how he called the merciful one 'pious' - it is not enough for him that he alone has mercy until others too have mercy - and the cruel one 'wicked'.

apparatus: Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads 'wants that he give and not others' as wanting all the good and praise for himself, and the miser as 'kilai'.

segments.english: There are four types in going to the house of study. One who goes but does not do: the reward of going is in his hand. One who does but does not go: the reward of doing is in his hand. One who goes and does is pious. One who neither goes nor does is wicked.

grammar: Pattern as in 5:13: four types, each defined by a pair of participles (הוֹלֵךְ, עוֹשֶׂה); the participles are subjects ('one who ...').
וְאֵינוֹ is אֵין with a 3rd masculine singular suffix: 'and he is not'; it negates the participle that follows.
הֲלִיכָה (a Mishnaic verbal noun, 'going') is contrasted with מַעֲשֶׂה, 'deed, doing'.
שְׂכַר ... בְיָדוֹ: 'the reward ... is in his hand', i.e. he holds it, it is his.
segments.note: The English keeps 'does' because the Hebrew word is עוֹשֶׂה. Bartenura (normative) reads 'does' in the first clause as 'learns, reviews and understands' (the one who goes to hear but does not study) and the second as one who studies at home; Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative) reads it as practising the commandments, the first as one who does not seek them out. The English leaves the word open; the reading is recorded rather than adopted.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: he goes to the house of study to hear but does not review and learn and does not understand ('does' read as studying).
Bartenura: he learns and reviews in a house of study that is in his own house ('does' read as studying; 'goes' as going out to the public house of study).
Rambam: the going to the house of study has four types; note that he called the one who increases in acquiring virtues pious and the one who is lazy about acquiring them wicked.
Rambam's long digression on intellectual and moral virtues, the mean and the extremes, and the terms 'pious', 'sinner', 'unlearned' and 'wise' does not bear on the plain sense of this mishnah.
Rabbeinu Yonah: 'does not do' does not mean he does nothing of what he heard, for then he would be wholly wicked; he does not seek out the commandments and does them only when they come to hand.

segments.english: There are four types among those who sit before the sages: a sponge, a funnel, a strainer, and a sieve. A sponge, because it absorbs everything. A funnel, because it takes in through this and lets out through that. A strainer, because it lets the wine out and retains the dregs. And a sieve, because it lets out the fine meal and retains the choice flour.

phrases.english: A sponge, because it absorbs everything
phrases.literal: 'sponge, that-it absorbing [obj] the-all'; Bartenura: absorbs clear and cloudy water alike

phrases.english: A funnel, because it takes in through this and lets out through that

grammar: The four types are first listed as nouns (סְפוֹג, מַשְׁפֵּךְ, מְשַׁמֶּרֶת, נָפָה) and then each is explained by a clause with שֶׁ ('because it ...').
The explanations use participles (סוֹפֵג, מַכְנִיס, מוֹצִיא, קוֹלֶטֶת) to describe a habitual action.
בְּזוֹ ... בְזוֹ, 'in this ... in that', is the Mishnaic use of זוֹ (feminine) as demonstrative pronoun; the antecedent is the two openings (or ends) of the funnel.
אֶת marks the definite objects of מוֹצִיאָה and קוֹלֶטֶת; it has no English counterpart.
מְשַׁמֶּרֶת (filter) and נָפָה (sieve) are fem. nouns, hence the fem. participles מוֹצִיאָה, קוֹלֶטֶת.
segments.note: The mishnah gives only the utensils; the commentators (Bartenura, Rambam) supply the application to the disciple: the sponge cannot tell truth from falsehood, the funnel forgets, the strainer keeps the worthless, the sieve keeps the valued. The English keeps the images without the application. On קֶמַח and סֹלֶת: for Bartenura and Rambam the קֶמַח that passes through the sieve is the fine powder and the סֹלֶת kept is the coarse, choice part, so the English says 'fine meal' and 'choice flour'. The 'this/that' of the funnel is rendered literally.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: above, the four types of disciples concerned memory and forgetting; now the mishnah concerns sound reasoning and sifting the valid from the invalid.
Bartenura: the sponge absorbs water, cloudy or clear; so one has a wide heart and accepts all he hears and cannot tell truth from falsehood.
Bartenura: a funnel is a vessel set on the mouth of a barrel or skin when filling it with wine or oil.
Bartenura: one takes in all he learns but as he swallows it so he spits it out.
Bartenura: the strainer lets out all he hears in the house of study and retains the worthless.
Bartenura: the sifted fine meal falls through and the coarse, valued סֹלֶת remains; so one can sort and clarify what he hears, retaining the true and letting go the false.

Rambam: the sponge (sea-wool) absorbs everything, true and false; the funnel is one who understands at once and remembers nothing; the strainer remembers the bad and forgets the true; the sieve lets out the fine dust and keeps the choice flour.

apparatus: Vilna reads ביושבי for בְּיוֹשְׁבִים (5:15.3) and הסולת for הַסֹּלֶת (5:15.33): spelling/word variants, no change in sense.

segments.english: Any love that depends on a thing: when the thing ceases, the love ceases. And that which does not depend on a thing never ceases. Which is the love that depends on a thing? This is the love of Amnon and Tamar. And that which does not depend on a thing? This is the love of David and Jonathan.
segments.literal: all love that-it hanging on-thing, ceasing thing, ceasing love; and-that-not-it hanging on-thing, not-it ceasing forever; which it love the-hanging on-thing, this love-of Amnon and-Tamar; and-that-not-it hanging on-thing, this love-of David and-Jonathan

phrases.english: Any love that depends on a thing
phrases.literal: 'all love that-it hanging on-thing'; 'thing' is דָּבָר, a cause or material object (Bartenura: the cause of the love)

phrases.english: when the thing ceases, the love ceases
phrases.literal: 'ceasing thing, ceasing love'; a conditional without a particle: when the thing ceases, the love ceases

phrases.english: And that which does not depend on a thing never ceases

phrases.literal: 'this love-of Amnon and-Tamar'; Bartenura: because of her beauty

phrases.english: And that which does not depend on a thing

grammar: The first saying is a conditional without a particle: בָּטֵל דָּבָר, בְּטֵלָה אַהֲבָה, '(when) the thing ceases, the love ceases'. Each predicate stands before its subject.

בְּטֵלָה is the feminine singular of the stative participle (verbal adjective) בָּטֵל, 'ceasing, void', and agrees with אַהֲבָה. The feminine perfect would be בָּטְלָה. The masculine בָּטֵל agrees with דָּבָר; it can be read as the same participle or as the stative perfect 'has ceased'.
וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ is 'and that which is not' (ש + אֵין + 3rd fem. sing. suffix): the headless relative stands for 'a love which ...'.
Question and answer: אֵיזוֹ הִיא ... זוֹ ..., 'which is ...? This is ...'; אֵיזוֹ is the feminine of אֵיזֶה, 'which'.
אַהֲבַת is the construct of אַהֲבָה: 'love of'.
segments.note: דָּבָר is kept as 'a thing' because it is general: the commentators explain it as the cause or object on which the love depends (beauty in Amnon's case; a lasting purpose for David and Jonathan). The pack's BDB entry for זֶה ('lamb') is the wrong word, so the demonstratives point to Jastrow's זֶה, 'this'. For בָּטֵל, Jastrow's sense 2 ('to cease to exist') is the right one; Jastrow cites this mishnah there. The BDB entry for תָּמָר has David's daughter at sense 4.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: love that depends on a thing does not last: when the thing that caused the love ceases, so does the love. Love not dependent on a thing that perishes but on a lasting thing, such as love of the righteous and the sages, never ceases.
Bartenura on Amnon and Tamar: because of her beauty.
Bartenura on David and Jonathan: to fulfil the will of their Creator, since Jonathan said to David 'You will be king over Israel and I will be second to you'.
Rambam: bodily causes pass away and what depends on them passes with them; when the cause of love is divine, namely true knowledge, the love can never cease because its cause is permanent.
Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): the love of Jonathan for David did not cease though he risked losing the kingship; the love of Amnon and Tamar needs no elaboration.

apparatus: Names: Amnon and Tamar: 2 Samuel 13; David and Jonathan: 1 Samuel 18-20, 2 Samuel 1:26.

segments.english: Every dispute that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end endure. And one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not in the end endure. Which is a dispute that is for the sake of Heaven? This is the dispute of Hillel and Shammai. And one that is not for the sake of Heaven? This is the dispute of Korah and all his company.

grammar: סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם: 'its end is to endure/be established'; the infinitive with לְ gives the outcome ('is destined to'), and סוֹף 'end' can mean outcome or goal.
Negative counterpart: אֵין סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם, 'it is not its end to endure'; אֵין negates the nominal clause.
לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, 'for the name/sake of Heaven': 'Heaven' is the Mishnaic reverent name for God.
מַחֲלֹקֶת (Vilna מחלוקת) is a Mishnaic feminine noun, 'dispute', from the root of 'division'; the pack's BDB entry glosses it as 'division, course', the nearest sense.
Question and answer: אֵיזוֹ הִיא ... זוֹ ...; the second case reuses the headless relative וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ.
segments.note: סוֹפָהּ is rendered 'in the end' so that the English keeps the ambiguity the commentators discuss: for Bartenura's first reading the disputants endure (Hillel's and Shammai's disciples did not perish, Korah's company did); in his second reading the aim of the dispute, the truth, is what endures. The English 'will in the end endure' allows both. Korah's dispute: Numbers 16.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: the disputants themselves endure and do not perish (neither Shammai's nor Hillel's disciples perished, while Korah and his company did). He also reports another reading: 'its end' is the aim sought, to attain the truth, which endures ('truth emerges from the argument'), as the law follows Beit Hillel.
Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): the disputants endure, argue about one thing today and another tomorrow, and the dispute continues all their lives; they are given length of days besides.
Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): the dispute not for the sake of Heaven ends at the first dispute, where the disputants die, like Korah's.

apparatus: Vilna reads מחלוקת, להתקיים, and שהוא for שֶׁהִיא: spelling variants, no change in sense (5:17.2, 7, 13, 16, 17, 21, 28).

segments.english: Whoever makes the many meritorious, no sin comes through him. And whoever causes the many to sin, they do not give him the means to repent. Moses was meritorious and made the many meritorious; the merit of the many rests on him, as it is said, Deuteronomy 33: "He performed the righteousness of the LORD, and His judgments with Israel." Jeroboam sinned and caused the many to sin; the sin of the many rests on him, as it is said, 1 Kings 15: "For the sins of Jeroboam (son of Nebat), which he sinned and which he caused Israel to sin."
segments.literal: all the-causing-merit [obj] the-many, not sin coming upon his-hand; and-all the-causing-to-sin [obj] the-many, not they-give-means in-his-hand to-do repentance; Moses merited and-caused-merit [obj] the-many, merit-of the-many hanging in-him, as-it-is-said (Deuteronomy 33) righteousness-of YHWH he-did and-his-judgments with Israel; Jeroboam sinned and-caused-to-sin [obj] the-many, sin-of the-many hanging in-him, as-it-is-said (Kings I 15) upon sins-of Jeroboam (son-of Nebat) which sinned and-which caused-to-sin [obj] Israel

grammar: זִכָּה (Piel/causative of זָכָה) 'made meritorious, caused to have merit' contrasts with the Qal זָכָה 'was meritorious': Moses was meritorious and made others so.
הַמַּחֲטִיא (Hiphil of חָטָא) 'one who causes to sin' parallels הַמְזַכֶּה; both are participles with the article used as 'whoever'.
אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ is an impersonal plural: 'they do not enable him' (Heaven does not supply him the means); the verb is Hiphil of ספק, 'supply, suffice', here 'give the opportunity'.
תָּלוּי בּוֹ, 'hangs on him', means 'depends on him / is credited to him'; it is the passive participle of תָּלָה.

The two proof-texts are Deuteronomy 33:21 and 1 Kings 15:30; the Hebrew's brackets give the chapter (and the optional name 'son of Nebat'). The Vilna text has the references in the margin as כא and ל.
segments.note: 'Merit' (זְכוּת) is kept as one English word through the mishnah for the pun on זָכָה / זִכָּה. תָּלוּי בּוֹ is rendered 'rests on him' to keep the sense 'depends on, is attributed to'; 'hangs' is given in the literal line. The impersonal 'they do not give him the means' is kept as an impersonal plural, as in the Hebrew. The pack lists no entry for the verb חָטָא or for the Hiphil of ספק, so those tokens carry no sense.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: no sin comes through him, so that he not be in Gehinnom while his disciples are in the Garden of Eden.
Bartenura: they do not give him the means to repent, so that he not be in the Garden of Eden while his disciples are in Gehinnom.
Bartenura: 'caused the many to be meritorious' - he taught Torah to all Israel.
Bartenura: the judgments that are with Israel are credited to him as if he had made them.
Bartenura: since the verse does not say 'for the sins of Jeroboam and Israel', learn that everything depends on Jeroboam.
Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): so that his disciples not be in Eden and he in Gehinnom, as it is written 'You will not leave my soul to Sheol, nor give Your pious one to see the pit' (Psalms 16:10).
Rabbeinu Yonah (not normative): 'the righteousness of the LORD he did' - he completed and kept the whole Torah, he and all Israel with him.

apparatus: Deuteronomy 33:21: צִדְקַת יְהוָה עָשָׂה וּמִשְׁפָּטָיו עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל.
1 Kings 15:30: עַל חַטֹּאות יָרָבְעָם אֲשֶׁר חָטָא וַאֲשֶׁר הֶחֱטִיא אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל. The mishnah text has בֶּן נְבָט in brackets.
Vilna reads וזיכה for וְזִכָּה (5:18.21), and gives the references כא (Deut 33:21) and ל (1 Kings 15:30) as words.
